report:
# EU AI Act Compliance Requirements for High-Risk AI Hiring Tools: Current Status and Enforcement

## Executive Summary

AI systems used in hiring and employment decisions are classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act, with comprehensive compliance requirements becoming mandatory on August 2, 2026. While the regulatory framework establishes significant penalties for non-compliance, no specific enforcement actions have been documented to date, leaving practical enforcement mechanisms unclear.

## Key Findings

### Classification and Scope
AI systems used in employment decisions, including recruitment, selection, job advertising, candidate evaluation, and performance monitoring, are classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act (high confidence). [What the EU AI Act Means for Staffing Businesses](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/what-the-act-means-for-staffing-businesses/), [High-Risk AI Under the EU AI Act: Does Your Software Qualify?](https://secureprivacy.ai/blog/high-risk-ai-eu-ai-act-checklist)

The regulation applies regardless of company size - there is no revenue threshold for high-risk AI classification, meaning even small startups using AI hiring tools are subject to regulation (low confidence). [High-Risk AI Under the EU AI Act: Does Your Software Qualify?](https://secureprivacy.ai/blog/high-risk-ai-eu-ai-act-checklist)

The EU AI Act has extraterritorial reach and applies to any AI system that affects individuals located in the EU (low confidence). [Initial Prohibitions Under EU AI Act Take Effect](https://www.quinnemanuel.com/the-firm/publications/initial-prohibitions-under-eu-ai-act-take-effect/)

### Compliance Timeline
High-risk AI system compliance requirements become mandatory starting August 2, 2026 (high confidence). [What the EU AI Act Means for Staffing Businesses](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/what-the-act-means-for-staffing-businesses/)

### Technical Requirements
Companies deploying high-risk AI hiring tools must implement mandatory risk assessments, technical documentation, bias testing, human oversight, transparency disclosures, and continuous monitoring (high confidence). [What the EU AI Act Means for Staffing Businesses](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/what-the-act-means-for-staffing-businesses/)

High-risk AI systems require conformity assessments and CE marking before being placed on the market (low confidence). [Conformity Assessments in the EU AI Act: What You Need to Know](https://www.holisticai.com/blog/conformity-assessments-in-the-eu-ai-act)

EU Declaration of Conformity must be maintained for ten years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service (low confidence). [Conformity Assessments in the EU AI Act: What You Need to Know](https://www.holisticai.com/blog/conformity-assessments-in-the-eu-ai-act)

### Prohibited Practices
Certain AI practices in hiring are prohibited, including emotion recognition, biometric categorization of protected traits, and social scoring features (low confidence). [EU AI Act and Hiring: 2026 Compliance Guide](https://www.hiretruffle.com/blog/eu-ai-act-hiring)

### Penalties
Non-compliance with prohibited AI practices can result in fines up to €35-40 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (low confidence). [Enforcement / fines in the European Union](https://intelligence.dlapiper.com/artificial-intelligence/?t=08-enforcement&c=EU), [Key Issue 1: Fines/Penalties](https://www.euaiact.com/key-issue/1), [Initial Prohibitions Under EU AI Act Take Effect](https://www.quinnemanuel.com/the-firm/publications/initial-prohibitions-under-eu-ai-act-take-effect/)

Non-compliance with high-risk AI system requirements can result in fines up to €10-20 million or 2-4% of total worldwide annual turnover (low confidence). [Key Issue 1: Fines/Penalties](https://www.euaiact.com/key-issue/1)

### Enforcement Actions
No specific enforcement actions or cases have been documented in the available sources, making practical enforcement mechanisms unclear.

## Contradictions & Uncertainties

Sources disagree on the exact maximum fine amounts for prohibited AI practices violations, with some citing €35 million and others €40 million. [Enforcement / fines in the European Union](https://intelligence.dlapiper.com/artificial-intelligence/?t=08-enforcement&c=EU) vs. [Key Issue 1: Fines/Penalties](https://www.euaiact.com/key-issue/1)

Multiple claims have low confidence levels (below 0.4), particularly regarding extraterritorial application, conformity assessment procedures, company size thresholds, prohibited practices, and penalty amounts.

## Knowledge Gaps

- No documented enforcement actions or practical examples of how authorities will implement compliance monitoring
- Specific technical standards and testing methodologies for bias testing and risk assessments are not detailed
- Exact conformity assessment procedures and requirements for high-risk AI hiring systems remain unclear
- Coordination mechanisms between national authorities across EU member states are not specified
- Transition periods or grandfathering provisions for existing AI hiring systems deployed before August 2026 are not addressed
- Relationship between EU AI Act compliance and existing GDPR requirements for hiring AI systems needs clarification

## Sources

report:
# EU AI Act Foundation Model Requirements vs. Current US Federal AI Policy Approaches

## Executive Summary

The EU AI Act establishes legally binding obligations for foundation model providers through a risk-based regulatory framework, while the current US federal AI policy landscape remains unclear following the revocation of Executive Order 14110 in January 2025. The EU approach mandates specific compliance requirements for General Purpose AI models, contrasting with what were previously voluntary US approaches.

## Key Findings

### Legal Framework Structure
The [EU AI Act establishes legally binding obligations for foundation model providers, while US approaches rely on voluntary compliance and agency guidance](https://www.3cl.org/the-eu-ai-act-and-usa-ai-gov-action-plan-a-legal-comparison/) (low confidence). The [EU AI Act uses a risk-based classification system with specific requirements for high-risk AI systems, while the US approach was sectoral and voluntary](https://globalpi.org/research/ai-regulation-across-the-atlantic-eu-ai-act-vs-u-s-ai-governance) (low confidence).

### EU AI Act Requirements for Foundation Models
The EU AI Act imposes specific obligations on General Purpose AI (GPAI) models. [EU AI Act requires General Purpose AI (GPAI) models to meet transparency obligations including technical documentation, training-data summaries, and copyright policy](https://www.dataversity.net/articles/comparing-eu-and-u-s-state-laws-on-ai-a-checklist-for-proactive-compliance/) (low confidence).

For higher-risk models, [GPAI models designated as systemic-risk must conduct model evaluations, adversarial testing, assess systemic risks, report serious incidents to EU AI Office, and ensure cybersecurity](https://www.dataversity.net/articles/comparing-eu-and-u-s-state-laws-on-ai-a-checklist-for-proactive-compliance/) (low confidence).

### Jurisdictional Scope and Enforcement
The [EU AI Act directly applies to any provider of general-purpose AI models operating in the EU, regardless of where the provider is based](https://carta.com/policy/ai-regulation/) (low confidence). In terms of regulatory stability, the [EU AI Act can only be repealed by the EU parliament or struck down by a court, while US Executive Orders can be revoked by another president](https://carta.com/policy/ai-regulation/) (low confidence).

### Regulatory Thresholds
The [EU AI Act has a lower computing threshold for foundation model regulation, covering a broader range of AI models than US approaches](https://carta.com/policy/ai-regulation/) (low confidence).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties

A significant contradiction exists regarding the current status of US federal AI policy. [US Executive Order 14110 on AI was revoked on January 20, 2025, making any current US federal AI policy approaches based on it obsolete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_14110) (low confidence), yet multiple sources in this analysis discuss EO 14110 as active policy.

All claims in this report have low confidence levels (below 0.4), indicating substantial uncertainty in the available information.

## Knowledge Gaps

- Current US federal AI policy framework following the revocation of Executive Order 14110
- Publication dates for all sources, making currency assessment impossible
- Official EU sources for AI Act requirements (all claims rely on secondary interpretations)
- Specific implementation timelines for EU AI Act foundation model requirements
- Current US federal agencies or regulations governing foundation model providers
- Enforcement mechanisms comparison between EU and current US approaches
- Compliance costs and practical implementation differences between jurisdictions

## Sources

1. [The EU AI Act and USA AI.gov Action Plan: A Legal Comparison](https://www.3cl.org/the-eu-ai-act-and-usa-ai-gov-action-plan-a-legal-comparison/)

report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act and Designated Notified Bodies

## Executive Summary

The EU AI Act establishes mandatory conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems, with requirements varying based on system type and available standards. While the legal framework for notified bodies is defined, no specific notified bodies have been publicly designated for AI Act conformity assessments as of the available research.

## Key Findings

### Legal Requirements for Conformity Assessment

High-risk AI systems must undergo conformity assessment procedures prior to being placed on the market or put into service (high confidence). [Article 16: Obligations of Providers of High-Risk AI Systems - EU AI Act](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/16/)

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometric systems), providers can choose between internal control procedures (Annex VI) or assessment by a notified body when harmonized standards or common specifications are applied (high confidence). [Article 43: Conformity Assessment](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/43/) and [AI Act Service Desk - Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)

Third-party conformity assessment by notified bodies is required for certain high-risk AI systems, particularly those used by law enforcement, immigration, or asylum authorities (low confidence). [Conformity Assessments under the EU AI Act](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)

Third-party assessment is also required when harmonized standards or common specifications are unavailable or not fully applied for biometric systems (low confidence). [Conformity Assessments under the EU AI Act](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)

### Requirements for Notified Bodies

Notified bodies must be established under member state national law, have legal personality, and meet organizational, quality management, resource, and cybersecurity requirements (high confidence). [Article 31: Requirements Relating to Notified Bodies - EU AI Act](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/31/)

Notified bodies must be independent of the AI system provider and any other operator with an economic interest in the AI system (high confidence). [Article 31: Requirements Relating to Notified Bodies - EU AI Act](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/31/)

Certificates issued by notified bodies must be drawn up in a language easily understood by relevant authorities in the member state where the notified body is established (high confidence). [Article 44: Certificates | EU Artificial Intelligence Act](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/44/)

Notified bodies designated under other Union harmonization legislation may use existing documents and certificates to support their AI Act designation procedure (high confidence). [Article 29: Application of a Conformity Assessment Body ... - EU AI Act](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/29/) and [AI Act Service Desk - Article 29](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-29)

### Assessment Procedures

Notified bodies conduct periodic audits to confirm continued compliance of AI systems (low confidence). [Conformity Assessments under the EU AI Act](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)

### Timeline

High-risk AI systems must comply with requirements by August 2, 2026 (medium confidence). [EU AI Act High-Risk Requirements: What Companies Need to Know](https://www.dataiku.com/stories/blog/eu-ai-act-high-risk-requirements)

## Contradictions & Uncertainties

No direct contradictions were identified between sources. However, several claims regarding specific third-party assessment requirements and periodic audit procedures have low confidence levels, indicating uncertainty in the available information.

## Knowledge Gaps

- **No Designated Notified Bodies Identified**: The research found no specific notified bodies that have been designated for AI Act conformity assessments.
- **Unclear Assessment Criteria**: The exact criteria determining when third-party assessment by notified bodies is mandatory versus when internal assessment is permitted remains unclear beyond the basic framework.
- **Limited Procedural Details**: The specific procedures and requirements for notified body assessments beyond basic organizational requirements are not detailed.
- **Designation Timeline**: The timeline and process for member states to designate notified bodies for AI Act purposes is not specified.
- **Integration with Existing Bodies**: The relationship between AI Act notified bodies and existing notified bodies under other EU harmonization legislation needs clarification.
